q: Steps for a very first colour correction?
a: 1. Open the Color Grading workspace and click a video clip in the Clips strip. 2. In the Primaries panel press Add Node (`grade.addNode`). 3. If the picture is flat, set the sequence's colour management and the clip's colour space first. 4. Drag the Gain wheel's ring up until the brightest part looks right. 5. Raise Contrast a little, then Saturation. 6. Press Bypass to compare before and after, and again to restore. Each step is one undo step.

q: ok and how do I compare it with the original?
a: Press Bypass in the Primaries panel to see the clip without the grade, and press it again to bring the grade back.

q: and if I overdid it?
a: Undo with Ctrl+Z: every change is one undo step, and a drag counts as one step however long it lasts. You can also lower Gain, Contrast or Saturation again by hand.

q: Can I build parallel nodes?
a: Yes. Right-click the node canvas and choose Add Parallel Node (`grade.addParallel`): a second node and a Parallel Mixer appear, and the mixer blends the two results 50 / 50 by default.

q: Why does a log clip need colour management?
a: A log clip squeezes highlights and shadows into a flat picture and uses a gamut (F-Gamut) wider than your screen. Grading numbers only mean the same from clip to clip if every clip is first translated into one working space; this fork uses DaVinci Wide Gamut / DaVinci Intermediate. Nodes work on the working space's signal, so the same numbers look different in a Rec. 709, Rec. 2100 or DaVinci Wide Gamut sequence.

In a DaVinci Wide Gamut sequence the log conversion happens regardless.

q: How is the final Rec. 709 picture made from a wide gamut grade?
a: In a DaVinci Wide Gamut sequence the working space is converted to Rec. 709 at the end with highlight roll-off (BT.2390 tone mapping), and colours outside Rec. 709 are desaturated into it, so very bright or saturated values fold in gently instead of clipping.

q: What are curves good for?
a: A curve maps brightness in to brightness out. Use it for contrast with a soft shoulder, for lifting only the shadows, or for pushing one brightness range toward a colour through a single channel.

q: How do I draw a curve on a node?
a: 1. Select a clip and a node, open Primaries and click the Curves tab. 2. Pick the channel: Y (brightness), R, G or B. 3. Add points on the line and drag them; a straight diagonal is neutral. 4. Reset curve straightens the current channel. 5. For a first contrast, make a gentle S: shadows slightly down, highlights slightly up. The node box then reads Curves (or Primaries + Curves).

a: Bend the top of the Y curve so the highlights roll off gently instead of rising straight to white: a soft shoulder. Keep the change small and check the bright areas.
